title: The clip that follows Stephen Miller: a Duke junior, Nancy Grace and the night two lacrosse players were arrested
dek: It aired April 18, 2006. It resurfaced when he was named deputy chief of staff, again in October, and again at 4:38 Saturday morning. What was said, what the record shows about “the only Duke student,” what happened to the case, and what the people who were there say it did to him.
body:
The video resurfaces every time Stephen Miller is promoted. Jack Posobiec posted it on December 14, 2024, the month Miller was named incoming deputy chief of staff: “18 years ago, only one Duke student went on mainstream media to defend the Duke lacrosse players,” he wrote. “His name is Stephen Miller” [10]. He posted it again on October 2 this year, with the same text, and Mediaite ran it as a flashback that evening [14][11]. And at 4:38 on Saturday morning, hours after Trump named Miller chief of staff, he posted it a third time, with the arithmetic corrected to 20 years and a new last line: he is now chief of staff of the White House [15]. By late morning it was being reposted on Instagram.

The clip is real. It aired on April 18, 2006, and the full transcript is on CNN’s site [1]. Here is what was said that night, what happened to the case afterward, and what the people who were at Duke say it did to the 20-year-old in the chair.

## April 18, 2006

That morning a Durham grand jury indicted Reade Seligmann and Collin Finnerty, both 20, on rape, sexual offense and kidnapping charges; they were arrested, booked and released on bail [1][8]. Five weeks earlier, on March 13, the lacrosse team had hired two dancers for a party at 610 North Buchanan Boulevard, and one of them, Crystal Mangum, told police she had been raped [8]. Three team captains had volunteered DNA and offered to take lie-detector tests; the police declined the tests [8]. On April 5 the coach resigned and Duke cancelled the season [8]. On April 10 the state crime lab’s DNA tests came back matching none of the 46 players tested [8]. The district attorney, Mike Nifong, who was facing a primary in May, had been making public statements about the case since late March [8].

Cable news had made the story its own. Nancy Grace, a former prosecutor with a nightly show on CNN Headline News, had said on March 31: “I’m so glad they didn’t miss a lacrosse game over a little thing like gang rape!” [12]. Nieman Reports later wrote that cable emphasized every sensational element of the case, “with former prosecutor Nancy Grace leading the charge” [13].

On the night of the arrests, Grace brought on a Duke junior identified as a member of the Duke Conservative Union [1]. Miller said he spoke “for many students” who were “very, very concerned that two innocent people may have possibly just had their lives ruined,” and asked her whether she was saying it was not possible they were innocent [1].

“Oh, good lord!” Grace said. A grand jury had heard evidence, she said, and without hearing from the victim, “you’re saying the grand jury is wrong, the victim is lying” [1]. “I’m not saying I’m convinced at all,” Miller said [1]. “Do you have a sister?” Grace asked. “I assume you’ve got a mother. I mean, your first concern is that somebody is falsely accused?” [1]

“Don’t tell me what my first concern is, please,” Miller said. His first concern on hearing the allegations, he said, “was that an innocent woman had been raped,” but as the facts came out “there was many irregularities and inconsistencies that troubled me” [1]. He cited a photograph time-stamped 12:03 a.m., before the alleged attack, that he said showed the accuser already bruised. “That’s not what ‘Newsweek’ says,” Grace answered [1].

The exchange that circulates is about a minute of that. The version Mediaite transcribed in October has Miller saying the case “was prosecuted as a witch hunt from the beginning” and “People presumed their guilt, and in America, we don’t do that” [11].

## The columns

Miller was not a random student. He wrote a column for The Chronicle, Duke’s student paper, called “Miller Time,” every other Monday: 25 bylines over 19 months, from “Welcome to Leftist University” in September 2005 to “Farewell” on April 23, 2007 [6][5]. The columns between were on the pay gap (“It’s not chauvinism. It’s chivalry”), Christmas (“Christmas is being banned”), affirmative action, multiculturalism, and, on April 5, 2006, Durham itself: “Durham isn’t a petting zoo,” an argument that students need not engage much with the city, published the day the lacrosse season was cancelled [5]. A classmate wrote in to call that one “one of the most spoiled-sounding, uppity things you can say” [16].

On the lacrosse case his columns rebutted the accusations point by point and insisted the players be presumed innocent until clear evidence showed otherwise [7]. In “Persecution,” published in August 2006 as the three awaited trial, he wrote that “our lacrosse team was railroaded” and that Durham’s district attorney “would rather hunt for witches than search for justice” [3]. He catalogued the DNA results, the accuser’s changing accounts and Seligmann’s alibi, criticized a professor who had called the party a racist assault, and urged students not to “rush to judgment and find our peers guilty in advance of the facts” [3]. He also named the television he thought had been fair: Fox’s “O’Reilly Factor” and “Hannity & Colmes” [3]. He appeared on O’Reilly’s program as well as Grace’s, The Chronicle reported in 2016 [4].

Posobiec’s line that Miller was the only Duke student to go on national television has not been independently verified, as the conservative site Twitchy noted when it carried the clip in 2024 [10]. What the record shows is that he was the one who kept going back. The American Spectator’s Robert Stacy McCain, in a twentieth-anniversary piece this year, called him “a lone voice crying in the wilderness” in the early weeks [9]. A 2018 American Thinker essay cast him as the case’s Zola [17].

## April 11, 2007

The case collapsed in stages. Nifong won his primary in May 2006 by 883 votes, and indicted the third player, David Evans, on May 15 [8][9]. On December 22 he dropped the rape charges but kept the kidnapping and sexual offense counts; in January he handed the case to the state attorney general, Roy Cooper [8]. On April 11, 2007, Cooper dismissed everything and declared the three men innocent, citing a “tragic rush to accuse”; the next day he called Nifong a “rogue prosecutor” [8][2]. Nifong was disbarred on June 16 for dishonesty, fraud, deceit and misrepresentation, removed from office two days later, and served one day in jail for criminal contempt on August 31 [8]. Duke settled with the three players for an undisclosed sum [8]. Mangum was convicted of second-degree murder in 2013 in the stabbing death of her boyfriend, and on December 11, 2024, in a podcast interview from prison, said she had “made up a story that wasn’t true” [8].

Miller was back on the show the night the charges were dropped. Jane Velez-Mitchell, guest-hosting for Grace, introduced him as the Duke student who “has been critical of this district attorney from the very start,” and observed that he had “been so angry in the past” and did not seem as angry tonight [2]. “I’ve been waiting a long time for this day,” he said [2]. He was not celebratory, he said, after “a terrible year-long ordeal”; “What I feel is a sense of relief” [2]. The delivery of justice, he said, had only begun: it was “crucial that Mike Nifong answer for his actions” and “pay a price for railroading these innocent people” [2]. He still had, he said, “the same sense of outrage that this kind of thing can happen in the United States of America” [2].

## What it did to him, according to the people who were there

Several accounts argue the case made Miller. McCain writes that the furor had “a radicalizing effect” on Duke students, Miller among them, and that Miller later said the rush to judgment reminded him of “totalitarian tendencies” he had seen growing up in Southern California [9]. The Chronicle, in a 2025 look back at his columns, said the scandal gave him “a national platform” [6]. John Burness, then Duke’s senior vice president for public affairs: “He always believed he was on the side of morality” [4]. David Graham, a later Chronicle editor: “He was kind of a lone wolf” [4]. Michael Hardt, a professor of romance studies who was on the faculty then: “Apparently the young Mr. Miller didn’t make much of an impression” [4].

In 2017, with Miller newly in the White House, The Chronicle measured the adviser against the student in a piece titled “From lacrosse fact to voter fraud fiction” [7]. The columnist who had demanded evidence and due process had just asserted, without producing any, that buses had carried voters into New Hampshire and that non-citizens and dead people were on its rolls, for which The Washington Post’s fact-checker gave him four Pinocchios [7]. K.C. Johnson, the historian who chronicled the lacrosse case, told the paper the change was for the worse; another observer said Miller had simply adapted his approach to a more skeptical audience [7].

Miller has never disowned the student in the clip, and his allies treat it as the origin story: a case in which the mob, the faculty, the prosecutor and the press were wrong and he was right. His critics point to the same clip for the opposite reason, that the lesson he took from Durham was not about evidence but about enemies. Both readings are on the record above. What is not in dispute is the night itself: a 20-year-old told a national television host that two innocent people might have had their lives ruined, she said “Oh, good lord,” and a year later the attorney general of North Carolina said the 20-year-old had been right [1][2][8].
